title: The Missing Middle: What Mezzanine Finance Actually Solves Before You Give Away Equity
linkedin:
A business asks its bank for more debt to fund an acquisition or a new site. The bank offers less than the plan needs, capped by serviceability and security, not by how good the growth story is.

The conversation almost always jumps straight to the other extreme after that: bring in an investor, sell a stake, raise the rest as equity.

That jump happens because of who's in the room, not because those are the only two options. Banks offer senior debt within their lending limits, full stop. Advisers who arrange equity raises are, understandably, inclined to talk about equity raises. Almost nobody has a reason to mention what sits between the two.

Mezzanine finance is debt that sits behind a bank's senior facility. It costs more in interest because it carries more risk, sometimes with a small equity kicker attached. But it behaves like debt: repaid on a schedule, over a defined term, then gone. It doesn't sit on the register forever the way an equity investor does.

For a business with provable cash generation and a specific, funded use for the capital, that difference is often worth more than the higher interest rate suggests on paper. Full ownership, full control, for the length of the arrangement.

It isn't the right fit for every growth story. But it's worth knowing it exists before assuming the choice is binary.

Quick question for business owners who've ever had a bank cap their lending below what a growth plan actually needed: did anyone mention the option between a bigger loan and selling a stake in the business?

Most owners only ever hear about the two extremes, because the people in the room each only offer one of them. Banks lend what they lend. Equity advisers talk about equity.

There's a middle option that behaves like debt (repaid, defined term, done) but doesn't need the same security a bank wants. It costs more in interest, but it protects something a lot of owners value more than the rate: still owning all of the business in five years.

Worth knowing it exists before the next capital conversation.
